name: Malawi Sena
confidence_why: Known only second-hand, as quoted in another work.
catalog_citation: Kiso, Andrea. 2012. Tense and aspect in Chichewa, Citumbuka and Cisena: A description and comparison of the tense-aspect systems in three southeastern Bantu languages. PhD dissertation, Stockholm University (urn:nbn:se:su:diva-79021), sec. 4.3.1 'Tone', p. 79 -- restating Torrend, J. 1900. Grammatica do Chisena: a grammar of the language of the Lower Zambezi. Chipanga: Zambezi Mission, sec. 24 p. 13 and secs 30-33 pp. 16-17; cross-checked against Anderson, W. G. 1897. An introductory grammar of the Sena language, spoken on the Lower Zambesi. London: SPCK, 'Accent' pp. 8-9. Torrend and Anderson describe Lower-Zambezi (Mozambican) Sena, catalogued under nucl1396.
catalog_locator: Kiso 2012 p. 79, sec. 4.3.1 'Tone', paragraph beginning 'Torrend (1900) observes'. Primaries re-read at: Torrend 1900 p. 13 sec. 24, p. 16 secs 30-31, p. 17 secs 31-33; Anderson 1897 pp. 8-9 'ACCENT'.
catalog_quote: Torrend (1900) observes a tonic accent in Cisena, in general occurring on the penultimate syllable of words. Tonic accents are usually defined as stress realised by an increase in pitch, i.e. these accents are not ‘tones’, but pitch accents. Torrend does not give a definition but states that he only represents the tonic accents in his grammatical description when they deviate from the general pattern on penultimate syllables. No differences in meaning that are expressed by means of tone are described.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent (tonic accent, realised as raised pitch/stress) falls on the penultimate syllable of the word; no lexical or grammatical tone contrasts are reported. This is Kiso's restatement of Torrend 1900 (Lower-Zambezi Sena), applied in a dissertation whose own Cisena data come from Nsanje, Malawi; Kiso adds no first-hand prosodic observation.
new_statements.exceptions: Kiso: Torrend marks accent only where it deviates from the penultimate pattern. Torrend 1900 sec. 32 p. 17 (primary, nucl1396): 'informal words' (ideophones/interjections) may carry the accent on any syllable; Anderson 1897 p. 9: affixes/enclitics count as part of the word and shift the accent.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement ('penultimate syllable of words'); no discussion of phrase-level penultimate lengthening or citation-form vs connected speech for the Malawian variety.
new_statements.identity_note: Malawi Sena (mala1475, swk) is the Nsanje/Chikwawa (Lower Shire) variety, split by ISO from Mozambican Sena (seh = Glottolog nucl1396 'Sena', already in the catalog via Anderson 1897). The only accessible statement filed under mala1475 is Kiso 2012, whose own Cisena consultants are from Nsanje, Malawi, but whose accent statement is a restatement of Torrend 1900, a description of Lower-Zambezi (Mozambican) Sena. Anderson 1897 (nucl1396 source) explicitly says his Sena area extends up the Shire to the Ruo, i.e. into present-day Malawi Sena territory, so the nucl1396 first-hand penultimate statements plausibly cover this variety, but no source specific to the Malawian standard was readable. Kishindo & Lipenga 2007 'Parlons cisena', despite its subtitle 'du Mozambique', reportedly describes Nsanje (Malawi) Cisena.

sources.citation: Torrend, J. 1900. Grammatica do Chisena: a grammar of the language of the Lower Zambezi. Chipanga. (archive.org grammaticadochis00torruoft) -- Lower-Zambezi (Mozambican) Sena, catalogued under nucl1396.
sources.note: Sec. 24, p. 13: 'The tonic accent in Sena, when not marked in writing, is always laid on the penultimate'; sec. 32 p. 17: formal words always have the tonic accent on the penultimate, informal words (ideophones etc.) may accent any syllable. This is the primary that Kiso restates; it describes the Lower Zambezi variety, not Malawi Sena specifically.

sources.citation: Anderson, W. G. 1897. An introductory grammar of the Sena language, spoken on the Lower Zambesi. London: SPCK. (archive.org) -- catalogued under nucl1396; intro p. 2 says the language is spoken 'up the river Shire as far as its tributary the Ruo' (i.e. into present-day Nsanje, Malawi).
sources.note: pp. 8-9: 'The accent in Sena invariably falls on the last syllable but one in a word'; affixes count as part of the word and shift the accent. Lower-Zambezi Sena, already used for nucl1396.
